youtube.description: In this episode you will explain base case and recursive case, trace a recursive call on the stack and fix a wrong base case, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Recursion · 1:19 Factorial · 2:26 The call stack · 3:10 Second program · 4:25 Recap · 4:55 Bug of the Day · 5:47 Challenge · 6:13 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today a function calls itself. It sounds strange, but it solves many problems with little code.

scenes.onScreen: "Recursion": numbered lines (1. A recursive function calls itself; 2. The base case stops the calls; 3. Each call has its own variables) and an analogy card: Russian dolls: open one, and a smaller one sits inside
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem. It needs a base case. The base case is the simplest problem, and it stops the calls. Each call has its own variables on the stack. When the base case returns, the calls finish one by one. Think of Russian dolls. You open one, and a smaller one sits inside. Recursion looks like magic, but it follows two simple rules. First, solve the smallest problem directly. That is the base case. Second, solve a bigger problem by using the answer of a smaller one. If you forget the base case, the calls never stop. The stack fills up, and the program crashes.
points: The base case stops the calls
Each call has its own variables

scenes.onScreen: factorial.cpp: factorial of five with recursion
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] This is the base case. When n is one or less, the answer is one. [HL 8] This is the recursive case. The answer is n times the factorial of n minus one. [HL 12] Main asks for factorial of five. Five times factorial of four. Four times factorial of three. This goes down to one. Then the answers multiply back up to one hundred and twenty. [HL 4] The factorial of five means five times four times three times two times one. [HL 5] Check the base case first. It stops the chain of calls. [HL 8] The function calls itself with a smaller number. The number goes down by one each time. Each call waits for the answer of the next call, and then multiplies.

scenes.onScreen: the stack grows to three calls, then unwinds
scenes.animation: Frames stack up with a thud and leave with a whoosh, one step per narrated sentence
scenes.narration: Watch the stack. Each call adds a frame. Factorial of three calls two. Two calls one. Now the base case returns one. The frames leave one by one. Two returns two. Three returns six. Main receives the answer. Notice that the frames pile up on the way down, and they leave on the way back. The answers are built on the way back. The deepest call answers first, and that answer grows with each return.

diagram.caption: the stack grows to three calls, then unwinds

steps.note: the base case: factorial one returns one
factorial two returns two times one, which is two
factorial three returns three times two, which is six

scenes.onScreen: sumto.cpp: a recursive sum from one to n
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The base case is zero. The sum of nothing is zero. [HL 8] Otherwise, the sum to n is n plus the sum to n minus one. [TRACK n=4] Sum to four is four plus sum to three. That goes on down to zero. [HL 12] The answer is ten. [HL 5] Write the base case first, always. It is the safe ending. [HL 8] Sum to four is four plus three plus two plus one, and then the sum to zero gives zero. A loop can do this job too, and it uses less memory. But recursion fits trees and puzzles well.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as sumto dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints ten. Check by hand. Four plus three plus two plus one is ten.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A recursive function calls itself. Two. The base case stops the calls. Three. Each call has its own variables. Four. Every recursive call must move toward the base case. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: The base case stops the calls.
Each call has its own variables.
Every recursive call must move toward the base case.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A wrong base case
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The program prints zero for factorial of five. The base case returns zero, and zero goes into every multiplication. The whole answer becomes zero. For a product, the base case must return one. The base case is the answer for the smallest problem. For a product, doing nothing means multiplying by one. For a sum, doing nothing means adding zero. Choose the base value that does not change the result.

scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a recursive function that prints the numbers from n down to one. Call it with four. Hint: print the number first, and then call the function with a number that is one smaller. Write your answer in the comments.

bug.why: The base case value goes into every multiplication. With zero, every product becomes zero. For factorial the base value must be one.
